description: We are a passionate team of students from INHA University in Tashkent, united by our shared interest in Earth and space sciences. We are fascinated by our planet, the universe, and the role of science and technology in understanding our world
summary:
FIREWATCH transforms 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into a consistent record of wildfire activity across Central Asia and beyond. Our project addresses a major challenge in long-term fire monitoring: different satellite sensors detect fires differently. Since 2012, VIIRS has detected significantly more small fires than MODIS, creating an artificial increase in recorded fire activity when combining their datasets. In Uzbekistan, this initially appeared as a nearly fivefold jump, even though actual fire activity had not changed.

After successfully testing the methodology across Central Asian countries, we expanded our analysis to other regions to explore its global applicability. FIREWATCH aims to provide more reliable long-term fire monitoring, helping researchers and environmental organizations distinguish real changes in wildfire activity from differences caused by satellite technology.
details:
What it does. Fire records for Central Asia break in 2012. That year NASA’s VIIRS sensor (375 m) joined MODIS (1 km). VIIRS detects many small fires that MODIS misses, so a simple splice of the two shows fire activity in Uzbekistan jumping more than four times overnight. Any trend that crosses 2012 is distorted. Firewatch turns 25 years of detections into one consistent record and lets anyone explore it on an interactive map.
How it works. We convert raw FIRMS hotspots into hexagon-days (H3 resolution 7, about 5 km², counted once per day), which removes about half of the resolution gap before any modelling. We remove static heat sources such as gas flares, oil fields and smelters (likely Tengiz, Zhanazhol, Temirtau, Almalyk) using FIRMS labels plus a persistence rule: active almost every month, mostly at night. We then fit a Poisson model linking monthly MODIS and VIIRS activity during 2012–2019, when both satellites flew, separately for each country, and apply it back to 2000. Every value comes with a conformal 90% range.
Does it work. In Kazakhstan the 90% ranges contain the true value 92% of the time when whole regions are held out (50% before our fix, on the same data), with 9.8% error on 2020–2025. Uzbekistan’s 2012 jump falls from ×4.32 to ×1.24. Against MODIS burned area (MCD64A1), an independent product, the harmonized record shows no break at 2012 in four of five countries. Tested on Portugal, Australia, Brazil, the USA and India: the method transfers, but each country needs its own coefficients.
Benefits and impact. Emergency services, environmental agencies, researchers and journalists can compare a fire season in 2003 with one in 2024 without being misled by a change of satellites. That matters for tracking whether steppe and crop burning in Central Asia is really declining, and for planning prevention where fires recur.
Creativity. Instead of comparing raw points, we count fire on a common hexagon grid, so both sensors are measured in the same unit. We treat persistent night-time “fires” as industry, not wildfire, and we show uncertainty openly instead of hiding it. The map uses NASA Black Marble night lights, captured by the same VIIRS instrument that is in our data.
Tools. Python (pandas, DuckDB, h3, statsmodels), FastAPI, React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, deck.gl, ECharts, Google Earth Engine; deployed as a static site on Vercel.
Factors we considered. MODIS orbit drift after 2020 (kept out of calibration), satellite outage days, gas flares that FIRMS sometimes labels as vegetation fires, honest validation on regions and countries the model never saw, and clear limits: 2002–2004 lies outside the calibration range, Kyrgyzstan overcorrects because it has few fires, and we measure fire activity, not intensity.
